text: Use breadcrumbs only when pages sit more than two levels deep.
Keep mobile headings tight enough that none wraps beyond three lines.
Use quiet banners for system-wide issues and reserve modals for problems that block the task.
Pair the hero headline with one primary button and at most one quieter secondary link.
Format dates the same way everywhere, using short month names rather than all-numeric dates.
Give icon-only navigation buttons accessible names, plus tooltips on desktop.
Keep completed checklist items readable and mark them with a check instead of striking them through.
Keep the header row sticky when a long table scrolls vertically.
Validate a field when the user leaves it, not on every keystroke.
Show an en dash for missing values, never a zero or a blank cell.
Order checkout steps as email first, then shipping, then payment, then review.
Place labels above inputs, left aligned.
Show money with its currency and two decimals.
Make the entity name in each row a link, and limit row-level buttons to one visible primary action.
Keep page titles under six words.
Place the cookie notice at the bottom and keep it from covering the primary button.
question: Should the notice be a full-width banner or a small card?

text: Explain the benefit of notifications on a screen before triggering the system permission prompt.
When one widget fails, show a short plain error with a retry button and leave the other widgets working.
Left-align text columns and keep their headers aligned the same way.
Follow the headline with one sentence explaining the benefit of filling the space.
Place the illustration or icon above the headline, never beside it.
Show every account as a row in one list; no hero numbers.
Leave generous whitespace between sections so each reads as its own beat.
Write button labels as the action they take ("Save changes", not "OK").
Stack columns in reading priority, with the headline first and the image second.
Draw forecasts with a dashed line so they read as different from actuals.
Order dashboard widgets from summary to detail, top to bottom.
Place the primary mobile action at the bottom of the screen, within thumb reach.
Ask for one thing per screen in long onboarding flows.
Ask one question per screen during onboarding.
Keep figures small and restrained; avoid big display numbers.
Format card numbers into groups as the user types.
Let success toasts dismiss themselves, but keep error notifications on screen until the user closes them.
question: How long should a success toast stay visible before dismissing?

text: Lead each section with one short headline and one line of support.
Use one accent colour, only for actions and selection.
Keep the close control for menus and sheets in the same corner every time.
Default new privacy and sharing settings to the most private option.
question: Should privacy defaults differ for team accounts?

text: Highlight the hovered row so the eye can track across a wide table.
List password requirements before the user types and tick them off as each is met.
Keep everything the user typed after a failed submit; never clear the form.
Limit top-level navigation to five items, with the main action set apart at the far end.
Scroll mobile pages vertically only, allowing horizontal movement just in labelled galleries.
Limit a guided tour to three tooltips, each one dismissible.
Repeat the primary call to action at the bottom of long pages.
After a failed submit, move focus to the first field with an error.
Alternate feature sections between image-left and image-right so long pages keep a rhythm.
State which email address the confirmation was sent to.
Crop product screenshots to the relevant part of the interface rather than showing the whole window.
Show password requirements before the user types, not after an error appears.
Place destructive actions such as delete account in their own section at the bottom.
Sort bar categories by value, largest first, unless the categories have a natural order such as time or stage.
Order navigation items by how often visitors need them, with pricing before company information.
Apply toggle changes immediately without a save button.
Add an info icon beside a metric name that reveals a one-sentence definition on hover or focus.
Show a progress label that names the current step out of the total, such as Step 2 of 4.
Postpone profile and account-detail questions until after the user has reached a first useful result.
Give empty state illustrations a text alternative, or mark them decorative when the headline already says it.
Use one accent for the focal series and neutral tones for the rest.
Centre empty state content within the area it replaces.
Give each feature section one headline, one short paragraph, and one visual.
Align the submit button with the left edge of the fields.
Use a left list of sections on wide screens and a single stacked list on narrow ones.
Tuck secondary row actions into an overflow menu at the end of the row.
Open the welcome screen with what the user can do, not with the product name.
Mark unread notifications with a dot and a bolder title, so colour is never the only signal.
Group footer links under three or four short column headings.
Show a sort arrow only on the active column, and reveal it on hover for the others.
Write errors in plain, human language and keep technical codes to a small line for support.
Put inline error text directly under the field it refers to.
Say what failed and offer a retry button when an empty state comes from an error.
Place labels above fields and never use placeholder text as the only label.
Let users toggle each notification category individually, with one master switch at the top.
Offer CSV export from a menu in the table's header corner, not as a loose button.
Lead every empty state with a headline that says what will live here.
Use a bottom sheet for secondary choices instead of sending people to a new page.
Keep the bottom tab bar to four or five destinations, each with an icon and a label.
Open the mobile menu as a full-screen layer rather than a small dropdown.
question: Should the full-screen menu slide in from the side or fade in?

text: End onboarding with a short success screen that names the next action.
Cap the setup checklist at five items.
Add a search field at the top once settings span many sections.
Give the dashboard a single primary button, such as "Create report", at top right.
Show skeleton rows that match the real column layout while data loads, instead of a spinner.
Set autofill attributes on every address and payment field.
State units once in the column header or axis label instead of repeating them in every cell.
Preserve entered data when the user goes back to a previous onboarding step.
Summarise plan differences in a comparison of no more than six rows before the full table.
Ask for sign-up only after showing the visitor something of value.
Group related fields under a short heading so the form reads as a few chunks.
Keep empty state body copy to two lines or fewer.
Show code in a monospace block with a copy button.
Keep notification titles to five words or fewer.
Add one line of helper text under a setting only when the label alone is ambiguous.
Remember each user's sort, filters, and date range between sessions.
Group notifications by day with the newest at the top.
Avoid disabled submit buttons; keep them active and explain what is missing when pressed.
Right-align numeric columns so digits line up for easy comparison.
Avoid carousels for key messages; show them in a static row or stack.
Prefer bars over pie charts whenever more than three categories are compared.
Make the whole row tappable for radio buttons and checkboxes, not just the small control.
Limit onboarding to three steps before the user reaches the product itself.
Match the mobile keyboard to the field: numeric for card numbers, email layout for email addresses.
Label the main button with the step's outcome, such as Create project, instead of Next.
Keep backgrounds neutral; use colour only for buttons and links.
Pair every status colour with an icon or a word so meaning never depends on colour alone.
Pair the primary button with a text link for learning more, never a second filled button.
Show three customer logos at most in the first proof strip instead of a long wall of them.
Write testimonials with the person's name, role, and a specific result.
Name exactly what will be deleted in the confirmation dialog for destructive actions.
Show a skeleton layout while content loads rather than a blank screen or lone spinner.
Offer guest checkout before asking anyone to create an account.
Group settings under plain-word section headings such as Account, Notifications and Privacy.
Tell users who can grant access when a list is empty because of permissions.
Open external links in the same tab unless leaving would lose form progress.
Put the FAQ below pricing and keep each answer under three sentences.
Place the change versus the previous period beside each headline number, using an arrow and a percentage.
Explain why information is requested in one sentence under the step heading.
Keep page header and navigation visible when content is empty.
Make tap targets comfortably large and leave clear space between neighbouring ones.
Pair closely related short fields on one row, such as city with postcode, or expiry with security code.
Show the full total including shipping and tax before the final step, never only on the last screen.
Order tooltip content as label, then date, then exact value.
Offer a clear filters button when a search or filter returns nothing.
Replace header-only empty tables with a proper empty state.
Use a single column for forms.
Keep chart gridlines faint and horizontal only.
Collapse the promo code field behind a 'Have a code?' link.
question: Should the promo field also stay collapsed on desktop, or only on mobile?

text: Don't blame the user: write 'We couldn't find that email' rather than 'You entered the wrong email'.
Let users edit any earlier step from the review screen without losing data entered later.
Provide a reset-to-default link per section rather than one global reset.
Confirm destructive actions with a dialog that names the item being removed.
End the page with a closing headline that restates the offer in one sentence, above the footer.
Put the primary action at the bottom of each step with a quiet skip link beside it.
Show the monthly price first, with annual savings stated as a note beside it.
Underline links in body copy so they read clearly as links.
Start bar chart baselines at zero so bar length stays honest.
Put page count and a rows-per-page selector at the bottom of paginated tables.
Name metrics in plain language and avoid internal jargon or undefined abbreviations.
Show each setting's current value in its list row before the user opens it.
Mark the current page in navigation with more than colour alone.
Show a brief confirmation message beside the control after a setting is saved.
Order settings sections by how often people use them, most common first.
Preselect the saved delivery address and show a 'Change' link beside it.
Abbreviate large numbers, like 1.2M, in summary cards, and show full values in tables.
Offer a "Compare to previous period" toggle instead of permanently drawing a second line.
Keep keyboard focus clearly visible on rows and sortable headers, and let arrow keys move between cells.
Lead the dashboard with the three or four numbers that answer the user's main question, before any chart.
Show when data was last updated beside the dashboard title, in relative words like "5 minutes ago".
Show the card brand icon once the number is recognised.
Use radio buttons when there are five options or fewer; switch to a dropdown beyond that.
Group related metrics into one card instead of scattering many cards that each hold a single number.
Place the email field first and the password field second.
Disable the pay button after one click and show a 'Processing' label to prevent double charges.
Show a faded preview of the filled state behind the empty message.
question: Should the preview be a static image or live sample data?

text: Make toggle state readable through an on or off label as well as position.
Show inline error messages beside the field, saying how to fix the problem.
Never launch a tour over the interface on first load; offer it through a prompt the user can accept.
Show a clear back control at the top left of every detail screen.
Use a single Save button for forms with text fields, disabled until something changes.
Keep filters in one row above the table and show each active filter as a removable chip.
Offer one primary button that creates the first item.
Truncate long cell text with an ellipsis and reveal the full text on hover and keyboard focus.
Give each chart a text summary of its main trend for screen reader users.
Group dropdown menu items under headings rather than letting the list scroll.
Keep column headers to one or two words in sentence case.
Put a 'Mark all as read' action at the top of the list.
Highlight one recommended plan and leave the other plans visually quiet.
Separate nothing yet from no results in wording, since the first invites creation and the second invites changing filters.
Use real product screenshots in feature sections instead of abstract illustrations.
Say what went wrong and how to fix it, in two short sentences at most.
Let users skip any step that isn't required to start using the product.
Give every empty state one clear action button.
Keep empty states to one short line of explanation and one action.
Place form labels above fields instead of using placeholders as labels.
Use a sticky header that shrinks on scroll rather than one that disappears.
Label chart lines directly at their endpoints instead of sending the eye to a separate legend.
Mark optional fields with the word 'optional' instead of marking required fields with asterisks.
Show progress as a step count, such as 'Step 2 of 4'.
Add an error summary at the top listing each problem as a link to its field.
Offer a search field and a link home.
Write toggle labels as the thing being switched, such as Email reminders, not as a command like Enable email reminders.
Ask for one piece of information per screen.
Show the result count beside the table title and update it as filters change.
Write empty states in friendly, plain language and never apologise for the emptiness.
Use axis-free sparklines inside table cells to show trends alongside the current value.
Cap a line chart at four series and group everything else under a single series labelled "Other".
Use toasts only for confirmations that need no follow-up action.
Keep the overview page to a small set of widgets and move the rest to dedicated detail pages.
question: How many widgets is too many on an overview page?

text: Prefer simple, sparse illustrations over busy hero graphics.
Give password fields a show and hide toggle.
Offer an undo toast instead of a confirmation dialog when a deletion is reversible.
Never say 'invalid' on its own; name the format the field expects.
Keep hero subheads to two lines or fewer.
Keep offline messages calm: say 'You're offline' and retry automatically once the connection returns.
Offer a skip option on every optional onboarding step.
Keep body paragraphs to a short line length that reads comfortably.
Explain why access is needed in a short pre-prompt before the system permission dialog appears.
Keep a search field visible in the header when the site has more than a handful of pages.
Let users show, hide, and reorder columns from a single columns menu.
Offer a density toggle with two options, comfortable and compact, near the table's top corner.
question: Should the density choice be saved per user or per table?

text: When rows are selected, replace the header with a bulk action bar that shows the selected count.
